newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. says troops still needed for Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says troops still needed for Zaire.

text.p: The United Nations said on Friday it was delighted that up to 400,000 Rwandan refugees were heading home from Zaire but insisted a multinational force was still badly needed to help provide aid.

But Rwanda's U.N. envoy and its ambassador to Washington told a news conference the planned force's mandate was now irrelevant and resources should be made available instead to help resettle the refugees inside Rwanda.

In Ottawa, a spokesman for Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said the humanitarian rescue mission, under the command of a Canadian general, would go ahead. "It's all systems go. We are still continuing with the plans for the mission as planned," the spokesman said.

The U.N. Security Council was meeting behind closed doors to discuss a resolution authorising the force to support delivery of humanitarian aid for more than a million refugees and their voluntary, orderly repatriation.
U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa told Reuters the Geneva-based U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees had called the huge exodus the "largest and fastest homeward movement of refugees in history."

"Everybody is absolutely elated but we still desperately need the multinational force," she said. "We have stocks in Rwanda for about 450,000 people but we are going to need a lot of help to move these people around."
Foa added that only a military operation could provide the required logistics.

Rwanda's U.N. envoy, Gideon Kayianamura, was also happy at the "good news" of the refugees' return but said he had asked the Security Council president and others involved "to rethink the mandate and the relevance of this multinational force in the circumstances."
"The much talked-about humanitarian tragedy of Rwandan refugees is now coming to an end. We need support to rehabilitate them inside the country," he said.

A U.N. official in Zaire said the Rwandan refugees had finally "broken loose" from captors who had prevented their return -- a reference to former Hutu soldiers and militia who had controlled camps housing hundreds of thousands of Rwandans who fled to Zaire in 1994 after the massacre of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
Kayianamura said Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu and government ministers were at the border to welcome the refugees home.
Rwanda's U.S. Ambassador Theogene Rudasingwa said: "The intervention is not relevant today."

He added: "The Rwandan government is insisting that whatever resources are available, including the tremendous resources that would have gone into supporting this multinational intervention, should be available in Rwanda so that we use them in a process that is definitely likely to be difficult in resettling the people in Rwanda."

The resolution that Security Council members had envisaged adopting on Friday calls for a four-month operation. It also expresses the intention of establishing a follow-on U.N. operation to take over from the multinational force.

In a letter to U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali outlining the operation to be commanded by Canadian Lt. Gen. Maurice Baril, Canadian U.N. envoy Robert Fowler said it would act under Chapter VII of the U.N. Charter, which authorises the use of force. But he stressed it was "not intended to interfere with the balance of military forces in the area nor to support the re-establishment of camps in which armed elements are able to operate."
This was a reference Zairian Tutsis who have been battling Zaire's army and to the former Rwandan soldiers and militia who had controlled the refugee camps.
